segments.title: HMS Neptune combines superfiring and wing turrets
segments.body: Neptune followed Dreadnought, Bellerophon, and St Vincent after the Royal Navy had accumulated several years of commissioning and operational experience. The sequence reflects a cycle of testing followed by another design. Neptune's superfiring after pair allowed four guns to cover the stern. The offset wing turrets still limited the practical broadside to eight guns and left only two guns firing forward. Mounting the fifth turret on the centerline and repeating the superfiring arrangement forward could have produced a ten-gun broadside.

evidence.note: The transcript compares Neptune with earlier British dreadnoughts and explains the firing arcs of her superfiring after pair and offset wing turrets.

segments.summary: Neptune's aft superfiring pair improved stern fire, while the retained wing turrets limited the broadside to eight guns and left only two firing forward.

segments.title: Neptune trades maximum armor for broader protection
segments.body: At roughly 20,000 tons, Neptune retained a 21-knot speed while redistributing protection. Her belt ranged from eight to ten inches, giving up Dreadnought's eleven-inch maximum for substantially more eight-inch coverage. Bulkheads varied between five and eight inches, while the deck gained at least half an inch and reached three inches at its thickest. Barbettes and turrets were also thicker on average. Four-inch guns replaced the earlier three-pounder secondaries, and the torpedo battery lost two tubes. Eighteen Yarrow boilers supplied 25,000 shaft horsepower.

evidence.note: The transcript compares Neptune's protection with Dreadnought and details her secondaries, torpedo tubes, speed, horsepower, and boilers.

segments.summary: Neptune spreads heavier protection across more of the hull, replaces three-pounders with four-inch secondary guns, and reaches 21 knots with 25,000 shaft horsepower.

segments.title: Exercises turn dreadnought experience into new designs
segments.body: Neptune was ordered in January 1909, but Colossus and Hercules did not follow until July. During that interval the Bellerophon class entered service and St Vincent commissioned, increasing the number of dreadnoughts available for testing. Britain could therefore exercise modern battleships against one another rather than judging them only against pre-dreadnoughts. War games let crews use unfamiliar equipment until they discovered its real capabilities, weaknesses, and operating methods. That practical feedback helps explain why the later ships were variations on Neptune rather than simple copies.

evidence.note: The transcript links the timing of Neptune, Colossus, and Hercules to commissioning experience, testing, exercises, and war games.

segments.summary: The interval between Neptune and the Colossus class shows commissioning trials, exercises, and war games feeding practical experience into rapid British design changes.

segments.title: Indefatigable follows a year of battlecruiser experience
segments.body: By 1909 the Royal Navy had commissioned all three Invincible-class battlecruisers and had between roughly six months and a year of experience with them. It then ordered Indefatigable as an evolved version of that first generation. She retained eight 12-inch guns and the offset wing-turret arrangement, despite the restricted firing arcs already apparent in British dreadnought layouts. Her machinery used thirty-one Babcock & Wilcox boilers and four direct-drive Parsons turbines, rated at 43,000 indicated horsepower. A speed of 25.8 knots gave her nearly five knots over contemporary British battleships, a margin the navy could judge from operating both types itself.

evidence.note: The transcript dates the Invincible-class commissioning experience and describes Indefatigable's guns, wing turrets, machinery, horsepower, and speed.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy ordered HMS Indefatigable after operating the Invincible class for months, making her an evolved second-generation battlecruiser rather than an isolated experiment.

segments.title: Battlecruisers support Britain's global commerce war
segments.body: Early battlecruisers were intended to choose their fights, using speed to avoid opponents they could not defeat. That made them less risky to iterate quickly than battleships, which were expected to stand in the line and fight comparable enemy ships. British planning also extended beyond a North Sea war with Germany to possible conflict involving France, Russia, the United States, or Japan. In that global setting the battle fleet could concentrate on blockades and strategic choke points while battlecruisers attacked or protected commerce. The later Australian and New Zealand ships reflected an imperial mission that could not be reduced to the Anglo-German building race.

evidence.note: Battlecruisers through selective engagement, commerce warfare, blockade, worldwide British commitments, and the later Australian and New Zealand ships.

segments.summary: Indefatigable's speed is placed within a worldwide British strategy in which battlecruisers pursue economic warfare while the battle fleet controls blockades and choke points.

segments.title: Florida-class centerline turrets challenge British design
segments.body: The US Navy designed the Florida class around cruising range, coal firing assisted by oil burners, and roughly 20,800 shaft horsepower. Its five twin 12-inch turrets were all mounted on the centerline, avoiding the partial batteries created by British wing turrets. Superfiring pairs forward and aft gave the design a strong theoretical broadside. The middle after turret, however, could not fire directly astern because the rearmost turret blocked it. Firing one same-level turret close past another would also expose the neighboring gun crew to severe blast, noise, and vibration. The arrangement therefore improved the firing arcs without making centerline mounting an automatic solution to every problem.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Florida-class fuel, power, cruising-range priorities, centerline turrets, restricted after fire, and blast effects between neighboring mounts.

segments.summary: The Florida class combines long-range machinery choices with ten centerline 12-inch guns, improving firing arcs while retaining a troublesome same-level after pair.

segments.title: Britain and America drive the dreadnought design race
segments.body: The numerical naval race and the competition to improve battleship design had different leaders. In this interpretation, the more intellectually significant exchange was developing between Britain and the United States rather than Britain and Germany. Florida's centerline battery is the immediate example of American designers testing a different answer to the same firepower problem. German ships entering service were often already overtaken by British designs under construction. Building totals and technical innovation therefore did not necessarily have the same leaders.

evidence.note: The transcript distinguishes the construction race with Germany from an intellectual design competition between Britain and the United States.

segments.summary: The familiar Anglo-German construction race is contrasted with a more innovative Anglo-American contest over dreadnought layout and fighting efficiency.

segments.title: Kawachi's mixed 12-inch battery complicates the dreadnought label
segments.body: Kawachi appeared to carry a uniform all-12-inch main battery, but the fore-and-aft twins used 50-caliber guns while the eight wing-turret weapons were 45-caliber pieces. The two types would not share identical ballistic performance, complicating the usual all-big-gun definition of a dreadnought. That limitation did not make the class harmless. About 25,000 shaft horsepower and turbine machinery supported a 21-knot speed on a normal displacement approaching 22,000 tons. The ships still had useful protection and enough heavy firepower that an opponent could not safely ignore them. Caliber alone did not determine whether a battery behaved as a genuinely uniform system.

evidence.note: The transcript explains Kawachi's two types of 12-inch gun and assesses the class's speed, machinery, armor, and combat significance.

segments.summary: Japan's Kawachi class had 12-inch guns throughout, but different barrel lengths undermined the uniform ballistic performance expected of an all-big-gun battleship.

segments.title: Triple turrets concentrate firepower on fewer hulls
segments.body: The Regia Marina introduced the triple-gun turret while France was still building Danton-class semi-dreadnoughts and Austria-Hungary had not yet fielded dreadnoughts. That timing challenges assumptions about which navies led technical change. Twin turrets suited a navy able to distribute guns across many hulls, but a smaller fleet benefited from increasing the hitting power of each ship. Four triples could provide twelve guns where four twins provided eight, while five triples could raise ten guns to fifteen. Such concentration made centerline mounting essential because triple wing turrets would worsen the wasted-firepower problem. The Italian choice connects turret technology directly to budgets, expected fleet size, and the need to fight while outnumbered.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces the Italian triple turret and explains how concentrating more guns per mounting benefits a navy with fewer hulls.

segments.summary: Italy's adoption of the triple turret shows how a navy expecting fewer hulls could raise each ship's hitting power by concentrating more guns on the centerline.

segments.title: Dante Alighieri turns Cuniberti's ideas into a fast battleship
segments.body: Dante Alighieri placed twelve 12-inch guns in four centerline triple turrets. The design applied Vittorio Cuniberti's earlier ideas about heavily armed, high-speed capital ships. Twenty-three water-tube boilers supplied four turbines developing about 32,000 shaft horsepower. The resulting 22-knot speed exceeded the contemporary British battle line by roughly one knot and made her a fast battleship for 1909. Italy therefore combined concentrated firepower and speed in a single hull rather than creating a separate battlecruiser type.

evidence.note: The transcript links Dante Alighieri to Cuniberti and describes her boilers, turbines, horsepower, 22-knot speed, and fast-battleship character.

segments.summary: Dante Alighieri combines four triple turrets with 32,000 shaft horsepower and a 22-knot speed, applying Vittorio Cuniberti's ideas to an unusually fast battleship.

segments.title: Mediterranean strategy favors fast battleships
segments.body: Italy did not need battlecruisers for worldwide commerce raiding or the defense of a far-flung maritime empire. Its principal problem was controlling the Mediterranean, where opponents would have to approach or pass through a comparatively confined theater. A fast battleship could cover the required area without sacrificing armor for a specialized high-speed role. A very large navy could divide pounding power and fast missions between battleships and battlecruisers, but a smaller navy had to maximize each capital ship's capability. Even a fleet of only nine or ten fast battleships could use a modest speed advantage to choose engagements against slower battleships. Battlecruisers, meanwhile, would be reluctant to fight ships carrying battleship armor and guns.

evidence.note: The transcript relates fast battleships to Italy's Mediterranean objectives, limited fleet size, engagement choice, and lack of a global battlecruiser requirement.

segments.summary: Italy's confined Mediterranean requirements and limited fleet budget made a fast battleship more useful than maintaining separate battleship and battlecruiser forces.

segments.title: Dante Alighieri delivers a clean twelve-gun broadside
segments.body: Dante Alighieri carried twelve 12-inch guns in four triple turrets, giving every main mounting a useful place in the broadside. None of the turrets superfired, but all were on the centerline rather than divided between the ship's sides. Firing outward reduced the danger of blast damaging the deck or superstructure. The turret-mounted secondary guns were another favorable feature. The layout shows how centerline concentration could turn the triple turret's paper firepower into a practical broadside.

evidence.note: The transcript praises Dante Alighieri's four centerline triple turrets, twelve-gun broadside, turreted secondaries, and reduced blast risk to the ship.

segments.summary: Four centerline triple turrets give Dante Alighieri a twelve-gun broadside without wing-turret blast striking the ship's deck or superstructure.

segments.title: Gangut combines Russian speed with a twelve-gun broadside
segments.body: Russia adopted a Dante Alighieri-like arrangement of four centerline triple turrets, giving the Gangut class twelve 12-inch guns. Twenty-five Yarrow boilers supplied four turbines that developed about 52,000 shaft horsepower on trials. Using unusually good trial coal, the ships reportedly reached 24.1 knots and blurred the line between battleship and battlecruiser. Sixteen 4.7-inch guns provided defense against destroyers and torpedo boats, supplemented by a three-inch anti-aircraft gun and four torpedo tubes. The belt could have been stronger, but the class was designed to deliver a large volume of heavy fire. Its speed and broadside showed how quickly Russia could return to major-warship competition after defeat in the Russo-Japanese War.

evidence.note: Gangut's Italian-influenced layout, boilers, machinery, trial speed, main and secondary batteries, protection, and postwar Russian significance.

segments.summary: The Gangut class follows the Italian centerline pattern with four triple turrets, high trial power, and a 24.1-knot performance that blurred battleship and battlecruiser categories.

segments.title: Laid down and commissioned define the fleet totals
segments.body: The fleet graphs use specific definitions for construction and service totals. A ship enters the under-construction total when it is physically laid down, not when a government merely orders it. It enters the in-service total only when it has commissioned and become an operational naval unit. This distinction prevents paper orders and incomplete hulls from inflating a navy's immediately usable strength. It matters when comparing fast-moving dreadnought programs in which ordering, laying down, launching, and commissioning occurred at different times.

evidence.note: The transcript defines under construction by laying down and in service by commissioning, rejecting orders or uncommissioned ships as equivalent fleet strength.

segments.summary: The series counts a warship as under construction only after laying down and as in service only after commissioning, separating orders from physical and operational reality.
